sections.title: Mental model — three ways humans sort

blocks.md: Machine sorting copies three things you already do with hands: **picking smallest item repeatedly** (selection), **swapping neighbors until line ordered** (bubble), **sliding new card into sorted hand** (insertion). Every fancy sorter later is one of these ideas made smarter.
**Sorted part grows from one end; unsorted part shrinks. Every basic sort tells this same story.**

steps: Selection: scan rest → find min → swap to front slot → front moves right
Bubble: walk left-to-right swapping wrong neighbors → biggest lands at end → end moves left
Insertion: take next unsorted value → slide left past bigger ones → drop into gap

items.q: Which method never touches an element it already placed?
items.explain: Each selection pass fixes one FINAL position. Bubble/insertion placements can change later.

items.q: Which method slides elements RIGHT to open a gap?
items.explain: Insertion shifts bigger cards right while hunting the slot.

sections.title: Counting work — same lens as Module 01

items: **Selection**: outer n rounds × inner scan up to n ⇒ pairs-style counting. Swaps tiny, comparisons heavy
**Bubble**: same pair-style worst day; early exit saves nearly-sorted days
**Insertion**: worst day pairs-style, but nearly-sorted day ≈ single pass

blocks.md: All three struggle when input big and scrambled — pairs-counting territory again. Smarter divide-and-conquer sorters arrive at L2; first master these three by hand.

items.title: Implement Selection Sort
items.statement: Code it, then print array after EVERY round.
hints: Track index of min, not value.

solutionCode.label: select the minimum index, swap once per round

items.complexity: Always n(n−1)/2 comparisons regardless of input, but at most n−1 swaps. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why track the index rather than the minimum value?
followups.a: You need to swap the element into place, and a value alone does not tell you where it lives. Storing the value would force a second scan to locate it — the index carries both pieces of information at once.

followups.q: Is selection sort stable?
followups.a: No. The long-range swap can jump an element over an equal one — [2a, 2b, 1] puts 1 first and sends 2a behind 2b. That is why S107 uses insertion sort, not selection sort, to demonstrate stability.

items.title: Bubble Sort + Swap Counter
items.statement: Sort ascending, output total swap count. Try {3,2,1} and {1,2,3} — explain difference.
hints: Sorted input = zero swaps + instant exit.

solutionCode.label: bubble with a swap counter and early exit

items.complexity: Worst case n(n−1)/2 comparisons and swaps; best case n−1 comparisons and zero swaps with the early exit. Space O(1).

followups.q: Compare {3,2,1} against {1,2,3}.
followups.a: Reversed input needs 3 swaps — it is the worst case, since every pair is an inversion. Already-sorted input needs 0 swaps and the early-exit flag stops after a single verification pass, making it O(n). The swap count is literally the inversion count of the input.

followups.q: Why does the inner loop shrink by `pass`?
followups.a: After pass p, the p largest elements have bubbled to their final positions at the end. Re-scanning them is wasted work. It does not change the O(n²) label but halves the actual comparisons.

items.title: Insertion Sort Descending
items.statement: Same algorithm, biggest first. Flip exactly ONE comparison.

solutionCode.label: one comparison flipped from the ascending version
solutionCode.py:
def insertion_sort_descending(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    a = a[:]
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] < key:     # '<' instead of '>': the ONLY change
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key
    return a

items.complexity: Worst case O(n²), best case O(n) on already-descending input. Space O(1). Stable.

followups.q: Why does the strict comparison preserve stability?
followups.a: The loop stops as soon as a[j] is not strictly less than the key, so an element equal to the key halts the shift and the key lands *after* it. Using `<=` would shift past equals and reverse their original order.

followups.q: What is the best case and when does it happen?
followups.a: O(n), when the input is already in the target order — here already descending. The while loop then fails immediately on every iteration, giving one comparison per element. This adaptivity is why insertion sort is used for nearly-sorted data and as the base case inside quicksort.

items.title: Sort Only Even Positions
items.statement: Elements at indices 0,2,4… sorted ascending; odd indices untouched.
hints: Copy evens out, sort, write back — or adapt loops stepping by 2.

solutionCode.label: extract, sort, write back on the same stride
solutionCode.py:
def sort_even_positions(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    a = a[:]
    evens = sorted(a[0::2])
    a[0::2] = evens                 # odd indices untouched
    return a

items.complexity: O(m log m) where m ≈ n/2 is the number of even positions. Space O(m).

followups.q: Why extract rather than sort in place with a stride?
followups.a: Standard sort routines assume contiguous elements; there is no stride parameter. Extracting gives you a contiguous view to hand to the library, at the cost of O(n/2) scratch space. Writing your own strided comparison sort would avoid the allocation but re-implement what the library already does well.

followups.q: What does index 0 being even mean for odd-length arrays?
followups.a: An array of length 5 has even positions 0, 2, 4 — three of them, one more than the odd positions. The extract-and-write-back loop handles this naturally because both loops use the same stride and stop at the same bound; hardcoding n/2 is where the off-by-one appears.

items.title: K Passes of Bubble
items.statement: Run exactly k bubble passes; print result. Observe k biggest values settled right.
hints: Outer loop capped at k, not n−1.

solutionCode.label: cap the outer loop at k

items.complexity: O(k·n) — k passes over n elements. Space O(1).

followups.q: What is guaranteed after exactly k passes?
followups.a: The k largest elements occupy the final k positions, in their correct order. Nothing is guaranteed about the rest. This is the loop invariant of bubble sort, and it is what makes "k passes" a meaningful partial result rather than an arbitrary stopping point.

followups.q: What is this partial run good for?
followups.a: Finding the k largest elements in O(k·n) without a heap. For k = 1 it is a max-scan; for small k it beats a full sort. Once k approaches log n, a heap at O(n + k log n) overtakes it.

items.title: Is Nearly Sorted?
items.statement: Count elements more than one position away from sorted spot; if ≤ k, declare 'nearly sorted'.
hints: This decides whether insertion is a smart real-world choice.

solutionCode.label: compare each element against its sorted position

items.complexity: O(n log n) dominated by sorting the copy. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why does "nearly sorted" matter in practice?
followups.a: Insertion sort runs in O(n·d) where d is the average displacement, so on nearly-sorted data it beats O(n log n) algorithms outright. It is why Timsort detects existing runs and why introsort falls back to insertion sort on small or nearly-ordered partitions.

followups.q: Why use lower_bound rather than the index directly?
followups.a: With duplicates, an element can legitimately belong at several sorted indices. lower_bound gives the earliest valid one, which yields the most generous displacement measure. Comparing raw indices would flag duplicates as displaced when they are merely interchangeable.

items.title: Stability Tester
items.statement: Sort pairs (score,id) by score using YOUR insertion sort; verify ids of equal scores stay original-ordered.
hints: Ties must NOT swap — strict comparison.

solutionCode.label: insertion sort on (score, id); ties must not shift
solutionCode.py:
def stable_insertion_by_score(v: list[tuple]) -> list[tuple]:
    """Sorts by score only. Equal scores keep their original relative order."""
    v = v[:]
    for i in range(1, len(v)):
        key = v[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and v[j][0] > key[0]:   # STRICT '>': equals stop the shift
            v[j + 1] = v[j]
            j -= 1
        v[j + 1] = key
    return v

items.complexity: O(n²) worst case. Space O(1). Stable by construction.

followups.q: Exactly which character makes this stable?
followups.a: The `>` in the while condition. With `>=`, an element equal to the key keeps shifting right and the key overtakes it, reversing the original order of equals. One character is the entire difference between a stable and an unstable sort.

followups.q: Why does stability matter beyond this drill?
followups.a: It lets you sort by multiple keys with repeated passes: sort by the least significant key first, then by the more significant one, and earlier orderings survive within ties. Radix sort depends on exactly this property, and it is why std::stable_sort exists as a separate function.

items.title: Min-Max in Fewest Comparisons (warm-up)
items.statement: Find both min and max; naive needs 2(n−1) checks — do better with pairwise trick (~3n/2).
hints: Process elements in PAIRS: compare pair first, then winners vs max, losers vs min.
Odd length: seed both with first element.

solutionCode.label: compare in pairs, then winners to max and losers to min
solutionCode.py:
def min_max_pairwise(a: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    n = len(a)
    if n % 2 == 0:                     # seed with the first PAIR
        lo, hi = min(a[0], a[1]), max(a[0], a[1])
        start = 2
    else:                              # odd: seed both with the first element
        lo = hi = a[0]
        start = 1
    for i in range(start, n - 1, 2):
        small, big = a[i], a[i + 1]
        if small > big:                # 1 comparison for the pair
            small, big = big, small
        lo = min(lo, small)            # loser only ever challenges min
        hi = max(hi, big)              # winner only ever challenges max
    return lo, hi

items.complexity: About 3n/2 comparisons versus 2(n−1) for the naive approach. Space O(1).

followups.q: Where does 3n/2 come from?
followups.a: Each pair costs 3 comparisons — one to order the pair, one for the loser against the current min, one for the winner against the current max — and covers 2 elements. That is 1.5 per element, versus the naive 2 per element from testing every value against both extremes.

followups.q: Why can the pair loser never be the maximum?
followups.a: It already lost to its partner, so its partner is at least as large. Any element that beats the loser is beaten by the winner, so testing the loser against max is provably wasted. Halving the search space per comparison is where the saving comes from.

items.title: Move Zeros to End (stable)
items.statement: Push all zeros right preserving non-zero order — do NOT use library sort.

solutionCode.label: write pointer collects non-zeros in order

items.complexity: Time O(n), one pass plus a tail fill. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is this a stable partition rather than a sort?
followups.a: It splits elements into two groups — non-zero and zero — while preserving relative order within each group. No comparison between elements ever happens, so it is O(n), not O(n log n). Calling sort here would be both slower and wrong, since it would reorder the non-zeros.

followups.q: The swap-based variant is often quoted — is it better?
followups.a: Swapping a[write] with a[i] achieves the same result and writes fewer elements when zeros are rare, since it skips the tail-fill pass. The two-phase version is easier to prove correct and touches each slot exactly once. Both are O(n); prefer whichever you can defend without hesitating.

items.title: Chocolate Distribution
items.statement: Pick m packets minimizing max−min difference given to students. Sort first, then sliding window of size m.
hints: After sorting, answer = min over i of a[i+m−1]−a[i].
Sorting converts chaos into adjacent comparisons.

solutionCode.label: sort, then the tightest window of size m

items.complexity: O(n log n) for the sort, then one O(n) window scan. Space O(1) beyond the sort.

followups.q: Why must the chosen m packets be adjacent after sorting?
followups.a: The cost is max − min of the chosen set. For any non-adjacent selection, replacing an outer element with one inside the span can only shrink the gap. So an optimal set is always a contiguous window in sorted order — that is what reduces a combinatorial choice to a linear scan.

followups.q: What does sorting buy conceptually?
followups.a: It converts "compare every subset" into "compare adjacent windows". Sorting is rarely the answer by itself; it is a preprocessing step that makes a greedy or two-pointer argument valid. That reframing is the transferable lesson here.

revisionCard: Selection: find-min + one swap per round; prefix becomes final
Bubble: neighbor swaps; tail settles; early-exit on clean pass
Insertion: slide-right + drop; loves nearly-sorted data
Stability = equal keys keep arrival order; strict comparisons protect it
All three = pairs-level worst case — big scrambled inputs need divide-and-conquer
sort() default ascending; custom lambda flips anything
